name: Three-piece suit

card.summary: A suit jacket, trousers and matching waistcoat that gives a formal, structured silhouette and defines the waist and chest line.
card.aka: suit with waistcoat; suit with vest

quick.overview:
A three-piece suit adds a matching waistcoat (called a vest in American English) to the jacket and trousers. The waistcoat covers the waistband and shirt front, creating a continuous vertical line and a snug, tailored torso.

People wear it to look more formal and put-together; a fitted waistcoat can emphasise a V-taper by drawing attention to the chest and narrowing at the waist. The style dates to 17th-century England and has come in and out of fashion since the 1940s.
quick.how: It is worn for interviews, weddings and formal events, with the waistcoat buttoned (traditionally leaving the bottom button open) and a fitted cut. Tailoring determines the effect: darts give more shape, while looser cuts hang straighter.
quick.risks: Fit is the main concern: a waistcoat that is too tight pulls at the buttons, and a three-piece is warmer than a two-piece in hot weather. There are no health risks beyond comfort.

lead: A three-piece suit consists of a jacket, trousers and a waistcoat cut from the same fabric. The ensemble traces to 17th-century England, when Charles II, following the court of Louis XIV, required courtiers to wear a long coat, a waistcoat, a cravat and breeches.[1]

For appearance, the waistcoat covers the trouser waistband and creates a clean line from chest to waist; tailors use darts and button placement to shape the torso and influence how tall the wearer looks.[1] Fit and cut therefore do much of the work of the look.

Waistcoats were almost always worn with suits before the 1940s, declined through the Depression, wartime rationing and central heating, and have since moved in and out of fashion.[1] On T Nation, lifters mention three-piece suits in the context of dressing well and dressing a muscular frame.[2][3]

chain: Waistcoat covers the waistband and defines the torso
angle.text: A well-fitted three-piece suit gives a formal, structured outline and a visible waistline. People wear it to look polished and, for lifters, to show off a tapered torso.

paras: The waistcoat, called a vest in American English, may have lapels or not. Tradition leaves the bottom button undone so the wearer can sit comfortably, and a watch chain was once threaded through a middle buttonhole.[1] Waistcoats were rarely worn with double-breasted jackets.[1]

Silhouette depends on cut, darts and button placement: darts give a stronger shape, while a sack suit without them fits straighter and looser. Button position relates to the natural waistline and so to apparent height.[1]

The three-piece ensemble began at the 17th-century English court. In the late 18th and 19th centuries formal dress was simplified, and rules later loosened into the modern lounge suit.[1] The waistcoat was nearly universal with suits before the 1940s and has returned periodically as a sign of formality.[1]
On T Nation, posters mention three-piece suits when discussing dressing for work, shoe and belt pairings and looking "dapper,"[3][4] and in commentary on a bodybuilder wearing one at a gala.[5]

timeline.event: Charles II requires a long coat, waistcoat and cravat at the English court, the origin of the three-piece ensemble.[1]
Waistcoats are almost always worn with suits.[1]
Waistcoat use declines with the Depression, wartime fabric rationing and central heating.[1]
